# How to Use This Book {.unnumbered}

You can read this book from beginning to end or enter through a decision you want to understand. It is written for advanced undergraduate and master's students, and for professionals who want evidence they can use. The main explanations stand on their own; optional notes provide additional theory, methods, and applications.

## Reading layers

Start with the chapter's opening situation and follow the main argument. **Research Lens** boxes and **optional research notes** develop formal models, measurement, or debates that you can return to later. An **Applied Module** extends the ideas into a particular domain.

A **Practice Lab** asks you to produce something: a forecast, a question, a decision record, a message, or a proposed change. Choose a manageable example and make the output specific enough to inspect. You can use a fictional case when a personal one would be sensitive.

**Footnotes** provide methodological details and qualifications that some readers may want to examine more closely. The main text identifies the study's comparison and outcome as part of explaining its result.

## The long-form journey

The seven parts expand from individual choices to interaction and the design of decision processes.

| Focus | Parts | Central task |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Individual choice | I–III | Understand how judgments form and how people choose under uncertainty, risk, and delay. |
| Social decisions and influence | IV–V | Examine interdependence, persuasion, communication, and connection. |
| Negotiated agreement | VI | Develop a joint decision among parties with different interests and alternatives. |
| Better decision processes | VII | Redesign behavior, choices, and organizational procedures, then examine the results. |

: The book's main reading route. {#tbl-long-form-journey}

## A recurring chapter rhythm

Chapters introduce a problem, develop an explanation, examine evidence, and give you a way to apply what you have learned. Before reading a result, pause when invited to make a prediction. Afterward, ask what you would now do differently and why.

## Use one recurring ethical audit

When you propose a message, intervention, or agreement, ask whose objective it serves, who benefits, and who bears the cost. Consider whether the people affected can understand the arrangement, refuse it, or seek correction. Unequal power can make apparent consent difficult to interpret.

Finally, decide how you would discover that the proposal is causing harm. [Appendix C](appendices/appendix-c-portable-course-tools.qmd#ethical-audit) collects the full ethical audit alongside the practical tools.

## Find your place in the book {#follow-the-highlighted-loop}

The preface's decision map distinguishes functions that are easy to confuse. Each part opens with a shorter map of its own questions, and chapter notes connect particular mechanisms to the wider process. These are reading aids; human thought can move back and forth among the functions. In the preface’s map, green arrows show where learning can prompt revision. The first box identifies the current inputs; action and learning can change what is available for the next decision.

Four terms retain consistent meanings:

| Term | Meaning in this book |
| --- | --- |
| **Interpret** | Work out what an observation, action, or message means in context. |
| **Predict** | Anticipate the consequences of an option, including uncertainty. |
| **Expectation** | A belief about what will happen; in some settings, that belief can also help change the outcome. |
| **Value** | Assess how desirable or otherwise important a predicted consequence is. |

: Vocabulary for following the decision process. {#tbl-navigation-vocabulary}

Chapter 4 also introduces the technical use of *prediction* in theories of perception and distinguishes it from forecasting future consequences.

## Use the recurring cases cumulatively

Several cases return as the analysis develops. A hiring decision lets us examine evidence, intuition, and group judgment. Supplier and employment negotiations let us carry the same facts from preparation into agreement design. A difficult workplace conversation connects interpretation to communication and repair.

When a familiar case returns, look for the new question it helps answer. [How to Read the Evidence in This Book](how-to-read-evidence.qmd#how-to-read-the-evidence-in-this-book) offers a short guide to evaluating the studies along the way.

## Reading routes

| Your interest | Suggested route |
| --- | --- |
| The complete argument | Read the seven parts in order. |
| Individual judgment and choice | Parts I–III. |
| Markets and finance | Parts I–III, then the markets chapter in Part IV. |
| Strategy and organizations | Parts I, IV, and VII. |
| Persuasion and communication | Parts I and V. |
| Negotiation | Part VI, drawing on Parts IV–V when needed. |
| Formal decision analysis | Chapters 1–2 and Appendix A. |
| Evolutionary explanations | Chapters 6 and 8, then Appendix B. |
| Designing or evaluating research | The evidence guide, then Appendices E–F. |

Appendix C is a practical-tool reference, and Appendix D helps you find the major examples. The concept index points to a concept's main explanation and selected later uses.

## Version and link policy

The version date identifies the current build. Some linked resources and applications change over time; the surrounding text supplies the central explanation so that a broken link need not interrupt your reading. Corrections are most useful when they identify the passage and the evidence that would change it.
